newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU worries about jobs, but can do little.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU worries about jobs, but can do little.

text.p: It is, by now, a ritual at European Union summits.
The leader of whichever country holds the EU presidency rises to address the final news conference.
"The European Union places as its highest priority the fight against unemployment," the leader says. "Unless we do something to create jobs, the Union will remain distant from its people."
Reporters listen politely, waiting for the leader to start talking about something more substantive, such as the planned single currency.
For at least four years now, EU leaders have made the fight against Europe's double-digit joblessness a priority for the bloc.
They have chiselled the struggle into summit conclusions, agreed objectives and even come up with something close to a public works programme calling for trans-European infrastructure projects.
Yet unemployment remains high -- at about 11 percent compared with just over two percent in the 1960s -- and the EU's response is tepid.
SUCCESS IN REVERSING UNEMPLOYMENT ELUSIVE
Many leaders have begun calling for an Employment Chapter to be included in the EU treaty as part of the inter-governmental conference (IGC) reforms.

At the most recent summit in Dublin in December, the leaders urged member states to develop more responsive labour markets, reinforce training and education and pursue solutions to increase the labour content of economic growth.
But Brussels-watchers say employment policy is primarily a national not a pan-European matter and modern politicians accept they can go only so far in directing the jobs market.
"They cannot do much. Unemployment is (related) to a set of social and fiscal policies that are set at a national level," said Daniel Gros of the Brussels-based Centre of European Studies.
INCLUDING JOBS IN EU TREATY PROBLEMATIC

The debate over an Employment Chapter in the EU treaty underlines the difficulty of creating a response among 15 countries. Such a chapter will not create one job, opponents say, but could raise unreasonable expectations on behalf of the EU public.

Those advocating a treaty chapter -- led by the Nordic EU members -- see the inclusion of jobs language in the treaty as a way of forcing the EU to consider the implications of its actions on employment creation.
They say it is an essential move for the EU to show its citizens it has some meaning to their everyday lives.

But opponents -- primarily Britain, with some backing from Germany -- see treaty language as worthless at best and an invitation to the EU to interfere in the market place or spend Despite objections, it is expected that a new treaty, to be agreed in June or a bit later, will contain some language about jobs. This could include the creation of an advisory committee to study employment policy.
But when push comes to shove, EU leaders have shown themselves to be exceedingly reluctant either to interfere in the jobs market or to hand over responsibility for jobs policy.
It is accepted that employment should remain mainly a matter for national governments, but that even they are limited in what they can do.
"Everybody wants to be seen addressing the problem," one EU diplomat said, "but nobody wants to create the illusion that acting at a governmental or European level is going to be a panacea."
Although the concept of trans-European networks as a way of priming the employment pump was agreed by an EU summit in December 1993, funding is still far from complete.
Moves by European Commission President Jacques Santer to push a strong Confidence Pact on jobs have been stalled since EU finance ministers refused to spend more than $1 billion.

This has left the Commission in a similar position to the leaders themselves -- deploring the state of unemployment, calling for more flexible labour markets, but having little ammunition with which to fight the battle.
In the long haul, most EU leaders hope, the problem of unemployment will be dealt with by other policies being forged by the bloc.
The single currency and the single market, it is argued, will create the robust economic growth needed to create jobs -- turning a priority into a reality.
